item.title: US stocks: S&P 500, Nasdaq close lower as Nvidia woes and rate-hike bets pressure US market
item.description: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq experienced declines on Friday, primarily driven by concerns surrounding Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. The tech sector faced increased pressure, particularly the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which fell significantly. Although inflation data suggested a slightly lower increase, expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes remained unchanged. Major technology companies, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, contributed to the losses in the sector.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq ended lower on Friday as Nvidia-related concerns weighed on technology stocks, while the latest inflation data did little to change expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes.The S&P lost 31.53 points, or 0.42%, to end at 7,560.87 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 230.13 points, or 0.91%, to 25,135.96. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 46.14 points, or 0.09%, to 52,343.23.Nvidia's shares fell and recorded their sixth straight week of declines, their longest streak since October 2012, after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday. He stepped down after revelations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for China. Nvidia’s board has approached Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor to Huang, the Financial Times reported.The leadership uncertainty has raised questions about the durability of the AI trade because of Nvidia’s central role in the industry’s expansion and its financial ties to several companies in the sector. AI stocks have been a main driver of the equity bull market.Also Read: Fed officials signal further rate hikes as inflation remains elevated“The tech trade, the AI trade, Nvidia is going to go through a period of volatility, and you’re going to see the bulls and bears kind of wrestle on where this narrative goes through the rest of the year ... there’s been a loss of confidence,” said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial in Troy, Michigan, according to Reuters.“The market and investors are trying to navigate what the AI theme looks like in the absence of Jensen Huang, who was basically the AI champion and willing to use Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund a lot of this AI expansion. That’s gone.”Despite the recent volatility, all three major indexes were on track to post weekly gains. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were set to end four-week losing streaks.The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.7%, with Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom among the biggest drags.AI cloud companies CoreWeave and Nebius also declined, while data-centre-related stocks IREN and Applied Digital traded lower.The losses came ahead of Anthropic’s highly anticipated initial public offering next week, which could test demand for established AI companies as investors consider shifting money toward the new entrant.For live updates on US Markets, click hereThe S&P 500 technology index fell 1.6%, making it the worst-performing of the benchmark’s 11 major sectors. Microsoft edged 0.4% higher as a global outage affecting products including Outlook and Teams began to ease.The Labor Department said US producer prices rose slightly less than expected in October but increased 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest annual gain since November 2022.The data did little to change expectations for a Federal Reserve rate increase of at least 25 basis points in December. Markets were also pricing in a roughly 10% chance of a larger 50-basis-point move, according to the CME FedWatch tool.Comments from several Fed officials this week suggested the central bank could consider a more aggressive path of rate increases as inflation pressures intensify.San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said Friday that her “bias” was that the central bank would need to raise its policy rate. Boston Fed President Susan Collins also said tighter monetary policy was coming because inflation remained high.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Fed officials signal further rate hikes as inflation remains elevated
item.description: Federal Reserve officials are signaling further interest-rate increases to combat persistent inflation pressures in the economy. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly expressed concerns about services inflation and its implications for future policy. Both Boston Fed President Susan Collins and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan emphasized the need for tighter monetary policies. They indicated the possibility of upcoming rate hikes to achieve price stability and mitigate inflation.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve policymakers signalled that further interest-rate increases are likely as stubborn inflation and rising business costs threaten to keep price pressures elevated, Reuters reported.San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said her “bias” was that the central bank would need to raise its policy rate, particularly because services inflation was moving in the wrong direction and showing signs of persistence.“We’re going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving,” Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event.The core Consumer Price Index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3% month over month in each of the past three months. That is well above the monthly increase of 0.2% or less that would be consistent with the Fed’s 2% annual inflation target.Daly said she was particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing was “not moving in the correct direction,” as that category tends to be persistent.“That’s a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, might pass that along to customers,” she added.The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September before holding it at a range of 3.75% to 4% in October. Markets widely expect quarter-point increases at the Fed’s December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings, although Governor Christopher Waller has raised the possibility of a half-point move in December.Daly did not comment specifically on the timing of future increases but said markets understood that the Fed adjusts rates in response to changing economic conditions.She is also monitoring consumer spending closely ahead of the December meeting.Collins sees tighter policy aheadBoston Fed President Susan Collins also said further tightening was needed because inflation remained high, suggesting that rates may have to rise more than she previously expected.“I think it’s clear the direction that monetary policy needs to go and I would think that soon some additional firming, tightening of policy is appropriate,” Collins said in an interview with Bloomberg Television.Recent inflation data have been unfavourable and indicate that price pressures are spreading across the economy, Collins said. “I think it may be that a bit of a tighter policy path than I had pencilled in a couple of months ago might be appropriate.”Collins declined to specify how quickly rates should rise or how high they should go.“I don’t want to get ahead in terms of how high we should go or how fast,” Collins said, adding that her “best-case scenario” is for “a careful adjustment of policy.” She acknowledged, however, that “there are scenarios where I might think about that somewhat differently.”Speaking while attending a housing conference hosted by the Boston Fed, Collins said restoring price stability was essential to a healthy housing sector, even if tighter policy caused some near-term pain. She also said financial markets appeared to be functioning well.Logan calls for stronger market-support toolsDallas Fed President Lorie Logan said inflation was too high and monetary policy needed to become more restrictive. Earlier in the week, she argued for at least two additional quarter-point rate increases, potentially in quick succession.Logan also said the US Treasury market was functioning “very well” despite bouts of interest-rate volatility and that banks had improved their access to emergency funding over the past three years.However, she called on the Fed to strengthen its tools for supporting Treasury-market functioning and providing liquidity to banks without working against monetary policy.“Especially in an economic environment where tighter policy appears necessary, I believe it is prudent for the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) to strengthen its tools for supporting market functioning without providing unnecessary economic stimulus,” Logan said at a Dallas Fed conference on bank funding.Logan, a former head of open-market operations at the New York Fed, said no intervention was currently needed. She warned, however, that intervening during a monetary-policy tightening cycle could complicate the Fed’s communications.“Historically, the Fed’s interventions to support market functioning have come at times when the FOMC also wanted to stimulate economic activity,” she said. “The same asset purchases could serve two purposes: providing monetary policy accommodation and supporting market liquidity.”“If Treasury market dysfunction emerged now, the FOMC would not have the luxury of using the same asset purchases to accomplish two goals,” Logan said.Logan further said that the banks had improved their access to contingent funding, which provides liquidity during periods of market stress, but should continue preparing to use facilities such as the Fed’s discount window.As services such as FedNow and private-sector payment systems expand, banks could face liquidity needs during weekends and holidays. With the Fed planning to extend its Fedwire Funds wholesale payment system to Sundays and weekday holidays, Logan said discount-window operations should also be expanded.“This is not a change any one Reserve Bank can make on its own,” she said. “I look forward to discussions with my colleagues about this possibility.”Logan also urged the Fed to develop the ability to centrally clear its repurchase, or repo, operations. “This would reduce the balance sheet costs of intermediation,” she said. “Funding from the Fed could then flow more efficiently to the broad market.”(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Cerebras stock jumps 23% on surprise profit, forecast hike, easing AI spending worries
item.description: Cerebras Systems experienced a 23% increase in stock prices after announcing adjusted revenue guidance for 2026. The company reported a quarterly profit of $29.82 million, surpassing analysts' expectations of a loss. Cerebras also revealed a significant rise in cloud and services revenue, driven in part by its OpenAI agreement. Additionally, the company has signed a cloud services deal with Microsoft, with more details to come.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: Shares of Cerebras Systems surged 23% on Friday after the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker raised its annual revenue forecast and reported an unexpected quarterly profit, signalling growing momentum in its challenge to Nvidia in the AI chip market, according to a Reuters report.Cerebras shares jumped 23.21% to $120.44 at the opening bell before paring gains.The rally could add more than $3 billion to the company's market capitalisation if the gains hold, helping offset concerns over elevated AI infrastructure spending and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia following reports of CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.For live updates on US Markets, click hereCerebras raised its 2026 adjusted revenue guidance to between $940 million and $960 million, compared with its earlier projection of $880 million to $890 million. The revised forecast also exceeds analysts' average estimate of $887.04 million, according to data compiled by LSEG.The company reiterated its target of tripling revenue in 2027 and disclosed that it had signed a cloud services agreement with Microsoft.Cerebras also reported a significant improvement in profitability. Adjusted profit stood at $29.82 million in the third quarter, compared with an adjusted loss of $10.86 million in the corresponding period last year. Analysts had expected an adjusted loss of $38.4 million, Reuters reported.The company's adjusted cloud and services revenue, which includes contributions from its OpenAI agreement, more than tripled to $144.9 million during the quarter.Also Read: Anthropic IPO to test Wall Street's appetite for AI stocksOn the earnings call, Chief Executive Officer Andrew Feldman said delivery delays under Cerebras' $20 billion multi-year agreement with OpenAI were caused by industry-wide shortages of land and power rather than constraints in chip manufacturing.Despite Friday's rally, Cerebras shares had fallen 47.2% from their May initial public offering price of $185 as of Thursday's close, highlighting the volatility surrounding AI chip stocks.The latest results and improved outlook provide a boost to Cerebras as it seeks to expand its position in the fast-growing AI computing market, where Nvidia remains a dominant player.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
